first_comment: What's the biggest "small change" a client has ever asked you for? 👇
text:
"Should be quick!" is how free work starts. 🙃

Difficult client series, part 2/5. When a client asks for "one more small change" that's really a new project, don't say no and don't do it for free. Say yes, as a paid add-on.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

My client asked for "one more small change". It's new work. Write my reply.
Say yes, but as a paid add-on: what our deal covered, what's new, the price, and when it's ready.
Friendly, confident, no apologies, under 90 words.
Say yes, then name the price. Never "no problem".

Our deal: [what you agreed, e.g. logo + business card, 2 revision rounds (both used)]

Add-ons: [new item + your price, delivery time]

Their message: "[paste the client's message]"

Swap the brackets for your own project. The last line of the instructions is the one that does the work.

🔖 Save this for the next "tiny tweak".
📤 Send it to a freelancer who always says "no problem".

Hard truth: most scope creep is the freelancer's fault, not the client's.

If the scope lives in your head or in a vague email, the client can't know where it ends. Say yes to the first free tweak and you've set the rule for every one after it.

Write down what's included and what isn't before you start. A boundary stated early feels professional. Stated late, it feels like a fight.

Do you put scope in writing first, or fix it as you go?

They asked for a proposal. You spent hours on it. Then silence.

That's lost time and a pipeline that looks fuller than it is. Just checking in doesn't fix it: it gives them nothing to answer.

Paste into ChatGPT or Claude:

Write a follow-up to a client who went quiet after my proposal. Avoid the phrase just checking in. Add one useful idea for their project, then end with an easy yes or no question. Under 60 words. Proposal summary: [paste]

Follow for part 4 tomorrow.

first_comment: How long do you wait before following up on a proposal? 3 days, a week, never? 👇
text:
"Just checking in" gives them nothing to reply to. 👻

Difficult client series, part 3/5. Your proposal went out, then silence. Instead of another nudge, send one new, specific idea for their business and end with an easy yes/no question.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

A client went silent [X] days after my proposal. Write a short follow-up email.
Don't write "just checking in" or "following up". Open with one new, specific idea for their business that wasn't in the proposal.
End with an easy yes/no question. Friendly, no pressure, no discount, under 80 words.
Give before you ask.

My proposal: [what, price, timeline]. Client: [name].

What I noticed since: [one real thing you spotted about their business, plus any deadline coming up]

The "what I noticed" line matters most. Spend 5 minutes on their site or socials and find one real thing.

Unpopular opinion: the fourth follow-up is for you, not for the client.

A proposal that goes quiet is usually a to-do that slid down their list, not a verdict on you. One follow-up with something useful is smart. After that you're chasing.

Send a closing note instead: happy to pause this, reach out whenever it's back on your list. Door open, your time back.

How many follow-ups do you send before you let go?

text:
Don't carry Friday's inbox into Monday. 📥

That unread pile is lighter than it looks. Most of it needs one of three things: a summary, a two-line reply, or a no. These 5 prompts handle all three:
1. Turn a 40-message thread into decisions, owners, and open questions
2. Write a 2-sentence reply from your yes/no (no "just circling back")
3. Decline politely, once, without over-apologizing
4. List who still owes you an answer, plus a one-line nudge for each
5. Pick your top 3 for Monday morning, so you leave Friday with a plan

Freelancer? Slide 6 shows who still owes you a reply, with a one-line nudge for each.

Bonus on slide 8: got a reply you keep rewriting? Turn it into a template with [BRACKETS] and reuse it every week.

first_comment: What's the vaguest feedback a client ever gave you? "Make it pop", "more modern", "I'll know it when I see it"? 👇
text:
"Make it pop" isn't feedback. It's a guessing game, and you pay for every wrong guess. 🫠

Difficult client series, part 4/5. Vague feedback sends you redesigning blind, round after round. Instead, turn their exact words into 3 either/or questions they can answer with one quick reply.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

My client's feedback on my [WORK]: "[THEIR EXACT WORDS]"
Turn it into 3 either/or questions so I can fix it in one round.
Write my reply: thank them, ask the 3 questions, under 80 words.
No defensiveness, no jargon.
Ask, don't guess.

What I made: [YOUR CHOICES: layout, colors, fonts, images].

Paste their words exactly as written. The vague phrase is the clue, so don't clean it up. Read the reply before you send it.

🔖 Save this for the next "make it pop".
📤 Send it to a designer stuck on round four.
➕ Follow. Tomorrow, the finale: revision number seven.

#freelancetips #freelancer #chatgptprompts #clientcommunication #designerlife

Unpopular opinion: vague feedback is a brief problem, not a client problem.

Clients aren't trained to describe design or copy. Make it pop just means they feel something is missing. Asking is your job, and guessing is the expensive way to skip it.

Turn the feeling into a choice: bigger or smaller, warmer or cooler, A or B.

Do you ask for examples before you start, or only after round one?

The contract said two rounds. You're on round seven. Nobody forced you: you just kept saying sure.

Say the count out loud, calmly, then offer a paid option. Paste into ChatGPT or Claude:

Client wants another revision. Our deal: [rounds agreed]. Rounds done: [number]. Extra rounds: [your price]. Write a calm reply: state the count first, then offer more as a paid option, end with one easy question. Under 80 words.

Follow, a new series starts next.

first_comment: Be honest: how many free revisions did you give on your last project? And did the contract say two? 👇
text:
Two rounds agreed. Six already done. Round seven isn't a favor, it's a conversation. 🔁

Difficult client series, part 5/5. Every "sure" to one more tweak is free work. Instead of saying yes on autopilot, state the count calmly, offer extra rounds as a paid option, and let the client choose.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

My client wants another revision. Write my reply.
State how many rounds we agreed and how many are done, then offer more as a paid option.
Warm, calm, no apologies, no blame, under 80 words. End with one easy question.
Count first, then offer.

Our deal: [WHAT YOU AGREED, incl. revision rounds]. Rounds done: [NUMBER].
Extra rounds: [YOUR PRICE].
Their message: "[PASTE IT]"

The prices in the video are just an example. Use your own, and check your agreement for the revision limit first. Read the reply before you send it.

Hot take: saying sure, no problem to extra work isn't kindness. It's an unclear answer.

The client hears free. You meant polite. Neither of you is wrong, and you're the one who pays for it.

Same warmth, clear terms: Happy to. That's an add-on, here's the price.

Which request did you say sure to that you'd take back?

Two nudges sent, nothing back. The third message is the one you keep putting off.

So write the whole ladder once, before you need it. Copy into any free AI chat:

Client hasn't paid invoice [#] for [amount]. Write 4 emails for 1, 7, 14 and 30 days overdue. Each firmer than the last, under 50 words. Day 14 asks for a payment date. No guilt, no threats.

first_comment: Honest question: how many days do you wait before the first reminder? And has "just checking in" ever actually got you paid? 👇
text:
Two reminders, zero replies, and your fingers are already typing "just checking in". 🧾

Don't write the third one from scratch. One prompt builds the whole chase in advance: day 1 assumes they forgot, day 7 makes paying easy, day 14 asks for a payment date, day 30 is the final notice. Each one firmer, none of them rude.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

A client hasn't paid my invoice. Write 4 short reminder emails, one for each day overdue: 1, 7, 14, 30.
Day 1: assume they forgot.
Day 7: make paying easy, list how to pay.
Day 14: ask them to confirm a payment date by [DAY].
Day 30: final notice, mention the late fee from our contract, give a [NUMBER]-day deadline.
Each one firmer than the last. Under 50 words each.
Never write "just checking in" or "following up". No guilt, no threats.
Firm on dates, soft on people.

Invoice: [NUMBER], [AMOUNT], [WORK]. Client: [NAME, COMPANY].
How to pay: [PAYMENT OPTIONS].
Late fee in our contract: [YOUR TERMS, or delete this line and the fee from Day 30].

The client and amounts in the video are made up. Only mention a late fee that's really in your contract, and check every date in the email before you send it.

Net 30 is an interest-free loan from you to your client. Most freelancers hand it out without being asked.

Late payers aren't always villains. Money just goes to whoever is easiest to put off. Shorter terms and a deposit make you less easy.

Try one line in your contract: Work starts after a 50% deposit. Balance due 7 days after delivery.

Net 30 or net 7: what do you actually use?

text:
Your pitch isn't bad. It's just about you. 👀

That's why it gets ignored, and why you rewrite proposals for hours. These 5 prompts make AI write about the client's problem instead:

2. A cold DM under 50 words that ends with an easy yes/no question
3. A proposal opener: their problem, your 3-step plan, the result
4. A follow-up that adds a new idea instead of "just checking in"
5. A calm reply to "too expensive" that cuts scope, not your price

The result: messages that give the client something easy to answer, written in minutes instead of hours.

first_comment: Paste the first line of your last pitch below. How many times does it say "I"? 👇
text:
Count the word "I" in the first line of your last pitch. Most of the line is probably about you. 📭

A client deciding whether to keep reading doesn't need your years of experience yet. They need a reason to read line two. So take your real first line, add one detail you noticed about them, and rewrite it around their business.

Copy-paste prompt (works in free ChatGPT, no login):

Here's the first line of my pitch: "[YOUR FIRST LINE]"
Rewrite it as 3 first lines about the client, not me.
Use only the details below. Don't invent facts, results or numbers.
Under 20 words each. No flattery.
No "I" in line one.

Client: [NAME, BUSINESS].
What I noticed: [ONE REAL DETAIL FROM THEIR SITE, POST OR JOB AD].

The client in the video is made up. Use a detail you really saw, and check it before you send. A better first line won't guarantee a reply, it just gives them a reason to keep reading.

Love your work is the same trap in a nicer coat. It says nothing the client can't hear from every other sender. A specific thing you noticed on their site does more than any compliment.

text:
You're not getting ignored. You're messaging the wrong people.

More pitches won't fix that. Picking who to pitch might. These 5 prompts come before you write a word:
1. List 10 types of small businesses that need what you do
2. Find where they spend time online, plus search phrases to type
3. Spot public signs that one of them needs you now
4. Score the businesses you found, and keep the top 5
5. Write one line on why you're contacting each one now, or skip them

Bonus on slide 8: a 2-line hello to a past client, your warmest list.

You end up with 5 real names, each with a reason, instead of a blast to 100 strangers.
